items.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Natalie Cole did not change — I mean she sang with Nat but they sang the Nat arrangement.

ctx.x: Well I think that’s what I told them, what I’ve been telling, I told RCA. I said, and if you look at it it’s obvious. Natalie Cole did not change — I mean she sang with Nat but they sang the Nat arrangement. Harry Connick had a big band and went around the world with it. And they were going ding-ding-a-ding. And Tony Bennett went on MTV and he went ding-ding-a-ding. They’re not stupid. People aren’t stupid. And that was the point, was I’m playing “Avalon” and I’m playing these fierce guitar solos and it sounds…

play “Avalon” by myself. And the kids are looking at me like where did he come from? They would have loved Joe Pass doing that same thing. If Joe Pass went in and did that for 17 year olds they’d go crazy. Or Tal Farlow. And so I always said you can get it to them. You don’t have to put me in a weird outfit and jeans and tell me not to wear a tie because they’re all — the tie, you know, you shouldn’t be wearing a tie and you shouldn’t be smiling God forbid. Nobody cares about that in the end. It’s about the…

items.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: you had Diana Krall and Natalie Cole and Harry Connick singing standards on the radio in the ‘90s

ctx.x: A few years ago my wife and I wrote a book based on these interviews and the publisher said, “Well first we want to know who’s your audience?” And for some reason I got a little annoyed with the question. I mean like well jazz people. I mean have you ever had a record label say that to you? Like who’s your audience? And should you do any adjustment of your song list and etcetera.

Well you know I try to make, I have a record that I’m trying to finish up of songs again from ‘60s, ‘70s, and ‘80s. I continually have these things because and I say I just made this “Stage & Screen” record and I really feel like we finally communicated what we do. It only took me, you know 33 years to sit on the stage and go oh, “Too Close for Comfort” and that, and feel like people are getting it. You know really on a wider stage than just say jazz people. I just felt like this is something that’s unique, how…

They want to know what you have to say. And they have, they’ve followed me through the Beatle record and through “Double Exposure” and the bossa nova records and tours of those things. I think the thing is not to make it a complete show. I would still say you’ve still got to play something here, something there, and in the middle you can promote the new album but I think it’s still like as opposed to making it an entire evening of one thing.
